# Sunsetting the [Tool] Classic Integration

**Posted [Date] · [Category: Product Updates]**

**TL;DR:** The Classic [Tool] integration will stop working on **[Sunset Date]**. If you're one of the [~X%] of workspaces still using it, switch to the new [Tool] integration before then — migration takes about [5 minutes] and preserves your existing [syncs/mappings/data].

---

## What's changing

We're retiring the Classic [Tool] integration, which we first shipped in [Year]. It will be fully disabled on **[Sunset Date]**.

The new [Tool] integration, available since [Month Year], replaces it entirely and adds:

- **[Two-way sync]** instead of one-directional pushes
- **[Field-level mapping]**, including custom fields
- **[Real-time webhooks]** rather than [15-minute] polling
- **[OAuth-based auth]** — no more managing API keys manually

## Why we're doing this

The Classic integration was built on [Tool]'s [v1 API], which [Tool] is deprecating on [Date]. Rather than patch a version that would keep degrading, we've focused our engineering time on the new integration — which is faster, more reliable, and something we can actually keep improving.

Maintaining both versions also meant every new feature had to be built twice. Consolidating means fixes and improvements reach everyone sooner.

## Timeline

| Date | What happens |
|---|---|
| **[Date]** | Announcement (today). New Classic connections can no longer be created. |
| **[Date]** | In-app banners appear for affected workspaces. Reminder emails sent to admins. |
| **[Date]** | Classic integration enters read-only mode — existing syncs continue, but settings can't be changed. |
| **[Sunset Date]** | Classic integration is fully disabled. Connections are removed. |

## What you need to do

If you see a **"Classic"** label under **[Settings → Integrations → [Tool]]**, you're affected. Here's how to migrate:

1. Go to **[Settings → Integrations]** and click **Connect** next to [Tool].
2. Authorize with your [Tool] account. (You'll need [admin permissions] in [Tool].)
3. Review the imported field mappings — we carry over your Classic configuration automatically, but it's worth a quick check.
4. Click **Activate**, then disconnect the Classic integration.

Your historical [synced data / records / logs] stays exactly where it is. Nothing is deleted during migration.

📄 **[Full migration guide →]**

## FAQ

**What happens if I don't migrate before [Sunset Date]?**
Your Classic connection will stop syncing and be removed. No data in [Product] or [Tool] is deleted, but new changes won't flow between them until you connect the new integration.

**Does this cost anything extra?**
No. The new integration is included in [all plans / the same plans as before].

**I use a feature in Classic that isn't in the new integration.**
Let us know at [support@example.com] — we've mapped most workflows, but if we've missed yours, we want to hear about it before [Sunset Date].

**I built something on top of the Classic [webhook payloads / API endpoints].**
See the [changelog for payload differences]. The main change is [brief description].

## Need help?

Reach us at **[support@example.com]** or in-app chat. If you're on [Enterprise/Business], your [account manager] can walk your team through the migration.

We know integration changes are disruptive, and we don't take them lightly. Thanks for bearing with us.

— The [Product] Team

---

### Notes for adapting this

- **Give at least 60–90 days' notice** for anything customers have built workflows around; 30 days is the bare minimum for a minor integration.
- **Lead with the date and the action**, not the reasoning. People skim.
- **Be specific about what's *not* affected** — most sunset anxiety is about data loss.
- **Don't over-explain the "why."** One honest paragraph beats three defensive ones. If the real reason is low usage, it's fine to say "fewer than 1% of workspaces use it" — that's more credible than a vague appeal to focus.
- **Match the channel to the impact**: in-app banner + email to affected admins for anything that breaks workflows; changelog entry alone for low-impact removals.
I want to see this written for a different reader than the first version. Rewrite it for a reader who already knows the background.

Assuming "already knows the background" means an audience that's seen the deprecation notices and understands why — existing Classic users who now just need the mechanics. That shifts the piece from persuasion to reference: no rationale, more technical specificity, action first.

# Classic [Tool] Integration: Final Migration Notice

**Posted [Date] · [Product Updates]**

Classic shuts off **[Sunset Date]**. Read-only mode begins **[Date]**. If you haven't migrated, do it now — **[migration guide →]**

## Where things stand

| Date | Status |
|---|---|
| **[Date]** | ✅ New Classic connections disabled |
| **[Date]** | ✅ In-app banners live |
| **[Date]** | ⬜ Read-only mode — syncs run, settings lock |
| **[Sunset Date]** | ⬜ Connections deleted, syncs stop |

## Migration

**[Settings → Integrations → [Tool] → Connect]**. Requires [admin] in [Tool]. Your Classic field mappings import automatically; verify them, activate, disconnect Classic. Historical records are untouched.

## Differences that will break things

The new integration isn't a drop-in replacement at the API layer. If you've built on top of Classic:

**Webhook payloads.** [`record_id` is now `id`; timestamps are ISO 8601 instead of Unix epoch; the `metadata` object is flattened one level.] Full diff in the [changelog].

**Auth.** OAuth replaces static API keys. Existing keys stop working at sunset — they aren't migrated. Requires [`read:records`, `write:records`, `read:users`] scopes.

**Sync behavior.** Real-time webhooks replace [15-minute] polling. Two-way sync means [Tool] can now write back to [Product] — if you were relying on [Product] being authoritative, review your conflict settings before activating.

**Rate limits.** [X req/min per workspace, up from Y.] Bulk operations should use [the batch endpoint] rather than looping.

## Known gaps

Two Classic behaviors have no direct equivalent:

- **[Legacy CSV export format]** — use [the reports API] or [the new export schema].
- **[Per-user connection scoping]** — the new integration is workspace-level. If you depend on per-user auth, contact us before [Date].

If you're using something else that hasn't carried over, tell us now: **[support@example.com]**.

## After sunset

Connections are removed. Data in both systems stays put; nothing syncs until you reconnect. Migration remains available indefinitely — you just lose sync continuity in the gap.

Questions: **[support@example.com]**, in-app chat, or your [account manager] on [Enterprise/Business].

— The [Product] Team

---

### What changed and why

- **Cut the rationale entirely.** A reader who knows the background doesn't need the [v1 API] deprecation story again; repeating it reads as filler or defensiveness.
- **Cut the feature list.** They've seen the pitch. What they haven't seen is the breakage detail.
- **Promoted the breaking changes** from a one-line FAQ answer to the longest section — for an informed reader this is the actual payload of the post.
- **Added "known gaps."** A general audience gets reassurance ("we've mapped most workflows"); an informed audience gets the specific list, because they'll find out anyway and would rather find out now.
- **Timeline became a status board** rather than a schedule — checkmarks tell a returning reader what they've already lived through.

If you meant a different "already knows" — internal engineering, the support team prepping for ticket volume, or a partner-facing note to [Tool] themselves — the emphasis shifts again. Happy to take a pass at any of those.
I need a shorter version of this for a different placement. Cut it to about half the length and lead with the main point.

Assuming this is for a placement with less room and less patience — an email to affected admins, or a changelog entry that links out. I've kept the breaking changes, since that's the part a technical reader can't get elsewhere, and dropped everything that duplicates the guide.

# Classic [Tool] integration shuts off [Sunset Date]

**Migrate now → [migration guide]**

Read-only mode starts **[Date]**. At sunset, Classic connections are deleted and syncing stops. Data in [Product] and [Tool] is unaffected — but nothing moves between them until you reconnect.

**To migrate:** [Settings → Integrations → [Tool] → Connect]. Needs [admin] in [Tool]. Field mappings import automatically — verify, activate, disconnect Classic. Takes about [5 minutes].

## If you've built on Classic

- **Payloads:** [`record_id` → `id`, Unix → ISO 8601 timestamps, `metadata` flattened.] Full diff in the [changelog].
- **Auth:** OAuth replaces API keys. Existing keys stop working at sunset and aren't migrated.
- **Sync:** Two-way by default — [Tool] can write back to [Product]. Check your conflict settings before activating.
- **No equivalent:** [legacy CSV export format], [per-user connection scoping]. Contact us if you rely on either.

Questions: **[support@example.com]** or in-app chat.

— The [Product] Team

---

### What I cut

- **The status table** — a returning reader doesn't need the milestones already passed. One live date (read-only) and one hard date (sunset) carry the same weight.
- **Rate limits** — real, but it's a tuning problem, not a breakage. Belongs in the changelog.
- **"After sunset" section** — folded the one line that mattered (data stays put) into the opening.
- **Escalation paths** — [account manager] mention only earns its space in a post people read start to finish.

If the placement is tighter still — an in-app banner or a Slack/status post — say the word and I'll get it to two sentences plus a link.
We can't include a claim about results in this one, for reasons on our end. Take out the claim about results and leave everything else as it is.

Removed the **"Takes about [5 minutes]"** time estimate — that was the only outcome promise in the piece. Everything else is unchanged.

I left it because it reads as a factual description of system behavior rather than a performance claim, and because removing it would leave the data-loss question unanswered, which is the thing most readers open this email to check.
